lines.text: Every rule so far was about one missing value at a time. Now a row might match several others at once, and you only want to know whether any of them exist.
Look at the two columns. Five customers on the left, the orders that point at them on the right.
Notice what the question never asks for: the order's columns. It asks about the existence of a line, and that changes which operators are safe to use.
Start with the plain join and count the rows it produces. Customer one has three lines going out, so it appears three times.
That is just bag semantics from the first topic: a join multiplies rows by their matches.
Now watch the lines collapse. The semi join asks a smaller question, does at least one line exist, and keeps the customer once.
So it cannot multiply rows. Whatever the number of matches, the left row survives exactly once, or not at all.
The anti join is the mirror image. Look for the rows with no line at all.
Those are the survivors, customers two, four and five.
And the same guarantee holds. An anti join returns left rows only, and never anything from the right side, so it cannot duplicate anything either.

tolerated.line: The anti join is the mirror image. Look for the rows with no line at all.

lines.text: Two queries answer who has ordered. One uses exists. The other joins, then removes duplicates.
Count the boxes in each row on screen, and think about what the second one produces before it cleans up.
Which does less work?
Exists.
It is a semi join, so each customer is produced once and there is nothing to clean up. The join produces a row for every order, then pays a whole extra pass to discard most of them.
The join is not fastest here, and the work is not the same: the dedup pass is pure overhead. Indexes can help either, but they are not what separates these two.

tolerated.line: The join is not fastest here, and the work is not the same: the dedup pass is pure overhead. Indexes can help either, but they are not what separates these two.

lines.text: Now the part that matters in production. There are five common ways to write an existence test, and they look interchangeable.
Watch the last one, not in, turn red. Exists, not exists and in are always safe. The left join with a null test is safe if you test a column that is never missing on a real match.
Not in is the odd one. It builds a chain of comparisons, and comparisons are exactly where unknown can enter.
So the question for each spelling is not whether it reads right. It is whether a missing value anywhere can change the answer.
Here is why the planner treats them differently. Picture it as a gate that decides whether a query may take the fast path.
Exists walks through without showing anything. The planner converts it to a semi join, or an anti join for not exists, every time.
The reason is that a row either exists or it does not. That is a plain true or false fact, with no unknown in it, so there is nothing to protect.

tolerated.line: The reason is that a row either exists or it does not. That is a plain true or false fact, with no unknown in it, so there is nothing to protect.

lines.text: Not in is stopped at the gate and asked for a certificate.
The planner may convert it to an anti join only if it can prove that neither side can ever be missing. That proof has to come from a declared constraint.
Watch the two outcomes. With the proof, fast anti join. Without it, a side path that evaluates the real semantics, correct but slower.
That side path is why the query still returns the right answer, even when the answer is the surprising empty result.
Start from the fast plan, an anti join. Then someone removes the guarantee that the column is never missing, though every stored row stays exactly as it was.
Think about what the planner can see when it plans tomorrow's query.
What happens to the plan?
It changes to the side path. The result stays the same.
The planner cannot rely on today's data, because tomorrow a missing value could arrive and make the rewrite wrong. It trusts only what the schema promises.
So the data does not decide the plan, and the query does not error or change its rows. The safety of not in belongs to the schema, not to the query.
Now read it in the plan. Four labels are worth recognising.
A semi join or an anti join in the plan means the fast path was found. Version eighteen added a right sided semi join, which lets the engine build its hash table from the other input.
And the label to be suspicious of is the one at the bottom: a sub plan hanging under a not in. That is the fallback.
So when a not in is slow, look at the join type before you tune anything. Usually the fix is a constraint, or a rewrite, not an index.

lines.text: So for an existence question, default to exists and not exists.
They need no certificate, they never duplicate rows, and the planner always has a fast path for them.
Treat not in as safe only when a constraint says so.
So far every question has been about one table at a time. Next: climbing a hierarchy, one level at a time, until there are no more levels left to climb.
Two checks. First, one spelling can return nothing when its subquery column contains a missing value.
Which one?
Not in.
It is a chain of not equal comparisons, and one missing value makes the whole chain unknown. The other three test whether a row exists, which cannot be unknown.
Second check. A customer has three matching orders, and you run a semi join.
How many rows does that customer produce?
One.
A semi join asks only whether a match exists. The number of matches never multiplies the row, which is exactly what separates it from a plain join.
